::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Algorithm to find critical points of function of two variables](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2338777/algorithm-to-find-critical-points-of-function-of-two-variables), asked by [Leonardo](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/164728/leonardo) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-06-27; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Given any function of $2$ variables such as $f=2x^2+3y^3$, would the following be the step by step method to find its critical points?
>
>  1. Differentiate it with respect to  $x$ (calling this $f_x$)
>  2. Differentiate it with respect to $y$ (calling this $f_y$)
>  3. Solve $f_x=0$ and $f_y=0$
>  4. Differentiate $f_x$ with respect to $x$ $(f_{xx})$
>  5. Differentiate $f_y$ with respect to $y$ $(f_{yy})$
>  6. Differentiate either $f_x$ with respect to $y$ or  $f_y$ with respect to $x$  ( the result should be the same i.e $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$)
>  7. Create a $2\times 2$ matrix as $$\begin{pmatrix} f_{xx}&f_{xy}\\ f_{yx} &f_{yy}\end{pmatrix}$$ substituting for every point possible found in step 3.
>  8. Find the determinant for the matrix.
>  9. If the determinant is $>0$ then this is a maximum, if it is $< 0$ it is a minimum.
>
> Correct?
:::

Everything is right except for step 9.  If the determinant is positive and $f_{xx} > 0$, the critical point is a maximum.  If the determinant is positive and $f_{xx} < 0$, the critical point is a minimum.  If the determinant is negative, the critical point is a saddle point.
